claim: Acute stress due to physical restraint induces stress-induced analgesia (SIA).
source: Specifically, acute stress due to physical restraint induces stress-induced analgesia (SIA).
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract, drawing on existing scientific knowledge about stress-induced analgesia.

claim: The dorsal lateral septum (dLS) facilitates SIA through its downstream targets in the lateral hypothalamic area (LHA) of mice.
source: Here, we describe how the dorsal lateral septum (dLS), a forebrain limbic nucleus, facilitates SIA through its downstream targets in the lateral hypothalamic area (LHA) of mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The dLS→LHA circuitry is sufficient to drive analgesia.
source: Taking advantage of transsynaptic viral-genetic, optogenetic, and chemogenetic techniques, we show that the dLS→LHA circuitry is sufficient to drive analgesia and is required for SIA.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic and chemogenetic manipulation experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: The dLS→LHA circuitry is required for SIA.
source: Taking advantage of transsynaptic viral-genetic, optogenetic, and chemogenetic techniques, we show that the dLS→LHA circuitry is sufficient to drive analgesia and is required for SIA.
evidence: This claim is supported by loss-of-function experiments using tetanus toxin to block neurotransmitter release.

claim: The dLS→LHA pathway is opioid-dependent.
source: Furthermore, our results reveal that the dLS→LHA pathway is opioid-dependent and modulates pain through the pro-nociceptive neurons in the rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM).
evidence: This is supported by naltrexone administration experiments that blocked the analgesic effects.

claim: The dLS→LHA pathway modulates pain through the pro-nociceptive neurons in the rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM).
source: Furthermore, our results reveal that the dLS→LHA pathway is opioid-dependent and modulates pain through the pro-nociceptive neurons in the rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing, photometry recordings, and manipulation experiments of RVM neurons.

claim: Inhibitory dLS neurons are recruited specifically when mice struggle to escape under restraint.
source: Remarkably, we found that the inhibitory dLS neurons are recruited specifically when the mice struggle to escape under restraint and, in turn, inhibit excitatory LHA neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by fiber photometry recordings showing dLS neuronal activity during struggle bouts.

claim: Activated inhibitory dLS neurons inhibit excitatory LHA neurons.
source: Remarkably, we found that the inhibitory dLS neurons are recruited specifically when the mice struggle to escape under restraint and, in turn, inhibit excitatory LHA neurons.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical evidence of inhibitory connections and photometry recordings showing inverse activity patterns.

claim: RVM neurons downstream of LHA are disengaged when dLS neurons are active, thus suppressing nociception.
source: As a result, the RVM neurons downstream of LHA are disengaged, thus suppressing nociception.
evidence: This is supported by photometry recordings showing reduced RVM activity during struggle and manipulation experiments.

claim: Descending modulation of pain is the mechanism through which the brain imparts control over somatosensory information processing in the spinal cord.
source: Descending modulation of pain is the mechanism through which the brain imparts control over somatosensory information processing in the spinal cord.
evidence: This is a well-established concept in pain neuroscience, cited from existing literature.

claim: Forebrain and midbrain regions encoding internal states such as stress and hunger can harness the brainstem circuits that project to the spinal cord neurons to alleviate pain.
source: Forebrain and midbrain regions encoding internal states such as stress and hunger can harness the brainstem circuits that project to the spinal cord neurons to alleviate pain (Tracey and Mantyh, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tracey and Mantyh, 2007.

claim: Direct electrical stimulation of the dLS has anti-nociceptive effects in humans.
source: Experiments involving human subjects in the 1950s and 1960s have shown that direct electrical stimulation of the dLS has anti-nociceptive (Gol, 1967; Olds and Milner, 1954) effects.
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical studies (Gol, 1967; Olds and Milner, 1954).

claim: In rats, dLS activation suppressed behavioral responses to foot-shocks.
source: In rats, dLS activation suppressed behavioral responses to foot-shocks (Breglio et al., 1970) or sustained noxious stimuli such as intraplantar formalin injections (Abbott and Melzack, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Breglio et al., 1970.

claim: In rats, dLS activation suppressed behavioral responses to sustained noxious stimuli such as intraplantar formalin injections.
source: In rats, dLS activation suppressed behavioral responses to foot-shocks (Breglio et al., 1970) or sustained noxious stimuli such as intraplantar formalin injections (Abbott and Melzack, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Abbott and Melzack, 1978.

claim: Septum inactivation or lesion renders rats hypersensitive to sensory stimuli.
source: Furthermore, septum inactivation or lesion renders rats hypersensitive to sensory stimuli, and as a result, they display exaggerated stimulus-driven defensive responses (Albert and Wong, 1978; Köhler, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Albert and Wong, 1978; Köhler, 1976.

claim: dLS neurons receive nociceptive inputs from the thalamus and somatosensory cortices.
source: dLS neurons receive nociceptive inputs from the thalamus and somatosensory cortices, as well as anxiogenic information from the hypothalamus (Chen et al., 2021; Menon et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2021; Menon et al., 2022.

claim: dLS neurons receive anxiogenic information from the hypothalamus.
source: dLS neurons receive nociceptive inputs from the thalamus and somatosensory cortices, as well as anxiogenic information from the hypothalamus (Chen et al., 2021; Menon et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2021; Menon et al., 2022.

claim: Neurotensin expressing dLS neurons with projections to the LHA mediate acute stress mediated suppression of food consumption.
source: Neurotensin expressing dLS neurons with projections to the LHA mediate acute stress mediated suppression of food consumption (Azevedo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Azevedo et al., 2020.

claim: Lesions to lateral parts of the septal nucleus resulted in a phenomenon known as septal rage.
source: Classical studies involving lesions to lateral parts of the septal nucleus resulted in a phenomenon known as septal rage, which leads to heightened defensive responses against non-threatening stimuli, indicative of increased levels of stress and anxiety (Brady and Nauta, 1953; Brady and Nauta, 1955).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brady and Nauta, 1953; Brady and Nauta, 1955.

claim: dLS is essential to sensing acute stress and instrumental in stress-induced fear and anxiety.
source: Interestingly, dLS is essential to sensing acute stress and instrumental in stress-induced fear and anxiety (Anthony et al., 2014; Rizzi-Wise and Wang, 2021; Sheehan et al., 2004; Terrill et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Anthony et al., 2014; Rizzi-Wise and Wang, 2021; Sheehan et al., 2004; Terrill et al., 2018.

claim: The involvement of dLS in acute stress-induced anxiety is reflected in behavioral phenotypes and elevated blood corticosterone levels.
source: This involvement of dLS in acute stress-induced anxiety is reflected in behavioral phenotypes and the elevated blood corticosterone levels (Singewald et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Singewald et al., 2011.

claim: The dLS neurons communicate primarily through their inhibitory neurotransmitters.
source: The dLS neurons communicate primarily through their inhibitory neurotransmitters and have prominent projections to brain areas involved in nociception and pain processing (Rizzi-Wise and Wang, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rizzi-Wise and Wang, 2021.

claim: dLS neurons have prominent projections to the lateral habenula (LHb) and the LHA.
source: Of note are the projections to the lateral habenula (LHb) and the LHA (Dafny et al., 1996; Shelton et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dafny et al., 1996; Shelton et al., 2012.

claim: The midbrain LHb can modulate the affective aspects of pain via its projections to the brainstem periaqueductal gray (PAG) and dorsal raphe.
source: The midbrain LHb can modulate the affective aspects of pain via its projections to the brainstem periaqueductal gray (PAG) and dorsal raphe (Shelton et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shelton et al., 2012.

claim: LHA neurons have strong connections to the pain-modulatory nuclei in the brainstem, such as the rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM) and the lateral parabrachial nuclei (LPBN).
source: LHA neurons have strong connections to the pain-modulatory nuclei in the brainstem, such as the rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM) and the lateral parabrachial nuclei (LPBN).
evidence: This is stated as established anatomical knowledge.

claim: LHA neurons can sense noxious stimuli and suppress pain.
source: In addition, recent studies have reported that LHA neurons can sense noxious stimuli and suppress pain (Siemian et al., 2021; Carr and Uysal, 1985), and specifically, the projections to the RVM were shown to have anti-nociceptive effects (Behbehani et al., 1988; Dafny et al., 1996; Franco and Prado, 1996; Fuchs and Melzack, 1995; Holden and Pizzi, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Siemian et al., 2021; Carr and Uysal, 1985.

claim: LHA projections to the RVM have anti-nociceptive effects.
source: In addition, recent studies have reported that LHA neurons can sense noxious stimuli and suppress pain (Siemian et al., 2021; Carr and Uysal, 1985), and specifically, the projections to the RVM were shown to have anti-nociceptive effects (Behbehani et al., 1988; Dafny et al., 1996; Franco and Prado, 1996; Fuchs and Melzack, 1995; Holden and Pizzi, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Behbehani et al., 1988; Dafny et al., 1996; Franco and Prado, 1996; Fuchs and Melzack, 1995; Holden and Pizzi, 2008.

claim: LPBN neurons are one of the primary targets of the ascending nociceptive projection neurons from the dorsal horn of the spinal cord.
source: Notably, LPBN neurons are one of the primary targets of the ascending nociceptive projection neurons from the dorsal horn of the spinal cord (Todd, 2010), and are instrumental in determining nociceptive thresholds (Chiang et al., 2020) and mediating nocifensive behaviors (Barik et al., 2018; Arthurs et al., 2023; Han et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Todd, 2010.

claim: LPBN neurons are instrumental in determining nociceptive thresholds.
source: Notably, LPBN neurons are one of the primary targets of the ascending nociceptive projection neurons from the dorsal horn of the spinal cord (Todd, 2010), and are instrumental in determining nociceptive thresholds (Chiang et al., 2020) and mediating nocifensive behaviors (Barik et al., 2018; Arthurs et al., 2023; Han et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chiang et al., 2020.

claim: LPBN neurons mediate nocifensive behaviors.
source: Notably, LPBN neurons are one of the primary targets of the ascending nociceptive projection neurons from the dorsal horn of the spinal cord (Todd, 2010), and are instrumental in determining nociceptive thresholds (Chiang et al., 2020) and mediating nocifensive behaviors (Barik et al., 2018; Arthurs et al., 2023; Han et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barik et al., 2018; Arthurs et al., 2023; Han et al., 2015.

claim: Mice subjected to restraint stress showed increased cFos expression in the dLS compared to control unstressed mice.
source: Mice that underwent RS showed increased cFos expression in the dLS as compared to the control unstressed mice (Figure 1A-C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: Most of the dLS neurons are inhibitory.
source: Since most of the dLS neurons are inhibitory (Figure 1D), we expressed the Gq-coupled excitatory Designer Receptors Exclusively Activated by Designer Drugs (DREADD) hM3Dq (Alexander et al., 2009) under the inhibitory neuron-specific Gad1 promoter (dLSGad1-hM3Dq-mCherry) (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Activation of dLS neurons by DCZ administration caused mice to exhibit stress and stress-induced anxiety-like behaviors.
source: When dLS neurons were activated by administration of i.p. DCZ (Alexander et al., 2009; Nagai et al., 2020), the mice exhibited stress and stress-induced anxiety-like behaviors as confirmed by blood corticosterone levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), the light-dark box test (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D), and the open field test (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays and corticosterone measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-F.

claim: Activation of dLS neurons suppressed nocifensive behaviors like licks on the hotplate.
source: Nocifensive behaviors like licks on the hotplate were suppressed post-DCZ administration in dLSGad1-hM3Dq-mCherry mice, with no changes in the jumping behavior (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H, I).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H, I.

claim: Activation of dLS neurons significantly increased tail-flick latency.
source: The tail-flick latency in these mice was significantly increased, the number of licks on the hotplate was reduced and the latency to lick initiation increased (Figure 1H, I).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1H, I.

claim: Mice with activated dLS neurons showed higher thresholds for mechanical pain.
source: Mice with activated dLS neurons showed higher thresholds for mechanical pain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by von Frey filament test data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The analgesic effects of dLS neurons lasted for up to 30 min post optogenetic activation.
source: Furthermore, it was seen that the analgesic effects of dLS neurons lasted for up to 30 min post optogenetic activation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), and this timeline was like the analgesic effects induced by RS (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by time-course data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The timeline of analgesic effects from dLS activation was similar to the analgesic effects induced by RS.
source: Furthermore, it was seen that the analgesic effects of dLS neurons lasted for up to 30 min post optogenetic activation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), and this timeline was like the analgesic effects induced by RS (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by time-course data comparing optogenetic and RS-induced analgesia shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: Silencing of dLS neurons prevented restraint stress from causing analgesia on the tail-flick assay.
source: Post-silencing of the dLS neurons, we observed that the stress caused by RS was unable to cause analgesia that was previously seen on both the tail-flick assay and the hotplate test (Figure 1K and L).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from TetTox-mediated silencing experiments shown in Figure 1K and L.

claim: Silencing of dLS neurons prevented restraint stress from causing analgesia on the hotplate test.
source: Post-silencing of the dLS neurons, we observed that the stress caused by RS was unable to cause analgesia that was previously seen on both the tail-flick assay and the hotplate test (Figure 1K and L).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from TetTox-mediated silencing experiments shown in Figure 1K and L.

claim: dLS neurons are both sufficient and necessary for SIA.
source: Concluding, that the dLS neurons are both sufficient and necessary for SIA.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combination of gain-of-function and loss-of-function experiments.

claim: dLSGad1-GCaMP6s neurons were active only when animals in the RS assay apparatus struggled and not when they were freely moving in their home cages.
source: Notably, in mice under RS, dLSGad1-GCaMP6s neurons were active only when the animals in the RS assay apparatus (see methods) struggled and not when they were freely moving in their home cages (Figure 2E, F, G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry recordings shown in Figure 2E, F, G.

claim: The increased neural activity during struggle bouts in mice under RS is not simply due to increased physical activity but due to the need and inability to escape the restraint.
source: This suggests that the increased neural activity during the struggle bouts in mice under RS is not simply due to the increased physical activity but due to the need and inability to escape the restraint (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing activity during struggle in restraint versus free movement, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: dLSGad1-GCaMP6s neurons were active during the initial immobilization phase while mice struggled during hand restraint.
source: Similarly, we restrained the mice acutely by hand, and dLSGad1-GCaMP6s neurons were active during the initial immobilization phase while the mice struggled, after which the activity was reduced when they were unable to move due to the restraint (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry recordings during hand restraint shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: dLSGad1-GCaMP6s neurons were active again when mice were released from hand restraint and were free to run away.
source: The neurons were active again when the mice were released from the hand restraint and were free to run away (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry recordings during release from hand restraint shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: The tail hanging assay engaged the dLSGad1-GCaMP6s neurons.
source: Another acute stress assay that engaged the dLSGad1-GCaMP6s neurons was the tail hanging assay, wherein mice were suspended in the air by holding their tails for 10 s (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry recordings during tail hanging shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: dLSGad1-GCaMP6s neurons were inactive during the hot-plate test at innocuous temperature.
source: The dLSGad1-GCaMP6s neurons were found to be inactive during the hot-plate test at innocuous (Figure 2H and I), as well as at a noxious temperature when the mice exhibited nocifensive behaviors such as licks and shakes (Figure 2J and K).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry recordings during hot-plate test shown in Figure 2H and I.

claim: dLSGad1-GCaMP6s neurons were inactive during the hot-plate test at noxious temperature when mice exhibited nocifensive behaviors.
source: The dLSGad1-GCaMP6s neurons were found to be inactive during the hot-plate test at innocuous (Figure 2H and I), as well as at a noxious temperature when the mice exhibited nocifensive behaviors such as licks and shakes (Figure 2J and K).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry recordings during hot-plate test shown in Figure 2J and K.

claim: dLSGad1-GCaMP6s neurons are preferentially tuned to stress caused by physical restraint and not to noxious thermal stimuli.
source: Thus, from our fiber photometry data, we concluded that the dLSGad1-GCaMP6s neurons are preferentially tuned to stress caused by physical restraint and not to noxious thermal stimuli.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the pattern of neural activity observed across different behavioral assays.

claim: dLSGad1 neurons have axonal targets in the LHA, the habenula (Hb), and the hippocampus.
source: In agreement with previous reports, we observed dLSGad1-GFP axon terminals in the LHA, the habenula (Hb), and the hippocampus (Figure 3C; Amit and Galina, 1986; Kubo et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 3C and citations to previous studies.

claim: dLS neurons synapse onto LHA, Hb, and hippocampal neurons.
source: To confirm that the axonal terminals of the dLS neurons at the targets form synapses with the neurons in the LHA, Hb, and hippocampal formation we labeled the axon terminals of dLSGad1 neurons with synaptophysin fused with the red fluorescent protein ruby (dLSGad1-SynRuby) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and found SynRuby puncta in all aforementioned dLSGad1 axonal targets (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that dLS neurons synapse onto its downstream LHA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), Hb, and hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is supported by synaptic marker labeling shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Selective activation of dLSGad1-ChR2 terminals in the LHA resulted in increased latency on the tail-flick assay.
source: Selective activation of the dLSGad1-ChR2 terminals in the LHA resulted in increased latency on the tail-flick assay (Figure 3E) and a reduced number of licks with an increased threshold on the hot-plate assay (Figure 3F), suggestive of analgesia.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic terminal activation data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Selective activation of dLSGad1-ChR2 terminals in the LHA resulted in a reduced number of licks with an increased threshold on the hot-plate assay.
source: Selective activation of the dLSGad1-ChR2 terminals in the LHA resulted in increased latency on the tail-flick assay (Figure 3E) and a reduced number of licks with an increased threshold on the hot-plate assay (Figure 3F), suggestive of analgesia.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic terminal activation data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Stimulating dLSGad1 cell bodies or their axon terminals in the LHA is sufficient to cause analgesia.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that stimulating dLSGad1 cell bodies or their axon terminals in the LHA is sufficient to cause analgesia.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from comparing the effects of somatic and terminal stimulation.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of dLSpre-LHA neurons had analgesic effects similar to dLSGad1 activation.
source: i.p administration of DCZ in the dLS pre-LHA-hM3Dq-mCherry mice had similar analgesic effects as seen with dLSGad1activation (Figure 3H and I), indicating that activation of a specific subset of dLS neurons (dLSpre-LHA) is sufficient for altering thermal nociception in mice.
evidence: This is supported by chemogenetic activation data shown in Figure 3H and I.

claim: Activation of a specific subset of dLS neurons (dLSpre-LHA) is sufficient for altering thermal nociception in mice.
source: i.p administration of DCZ in the dLS pre-LHA-hM3Dq-mCherry mice had similar analgesic effects as seen with dLSGad1activation (Figure 3H and I), indicating that activation of a specific subset of dLS neurons (dLSpre-LHA) is sufficient for altering thermal nociception in mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the projection-specific chemogenetic activation experiments.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of LHApost-dLS neurons reduced the latency to react on the tail-flick assay.
source: I.p. administration of DCZ in mice expressing hM3Dq in LHApost-dLS neurons reduced the latency to react on the tail-flick assay, increased the number of licks, and decreased the latency to lick on the hot-plate test (Figure 3K and L).
evidence: This is supported by chemogenetic activation data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of LHApost-dLS neurons increased the number of licks on the hot-plate test.
source: I.p. administration of DCZ in mice expressing hM3Dq in LHApost-dLS neurons reduced the latency to react on the tail-flick assay, increased the number of licks, and decreased the latency to lick on the hot-plate test (Figure 3K and L).
evidence: This is supported by chemogenetic activation data shown in Figure 3K and L.

claim: When activated, dLSGad1 neurons inhibit LHA neurons to cause analgesia.
source: Intriguingly, our data suggest that when activated, dLSGad1 neurons inhibit LHA neurons to cause analgesia, and so when LHApost-dLS neurons are artificially activated, it has the opposite effect on nocifensive behaviors and leads to hyperalgesia.
evidence: This is inferred from the opposite effects of activating dLS versus LHA neurons.

claim: When LHApost-dLS neurons are artificially activated, it leads to hyperalgesia.
source: Intriguingly, our data suggest that when activated, dLSGad1 neurons inhibit LHA neurons to cause analgesia, and so when LHApost-dLS neurons are artificially activated, it has the opposite effect on nocifensive behaviors and leads to hyperalgesia.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral effects of LHApost-dLS activation shown in Figure 3K and L.

claim: Activating Hb neurons post-synaptic to dLS (Hbpost-dLS) did not alter thermal pain thresholds.
source: DCZ administration had no effect on thermal pain thresholds in Hbpost-dLS-hM3Dq mice (Figure 3N and O).
evidence: This is supported by chemogenetic activation data shown in Figure 3N and O.

claim: TetTox-mediated LHApost-dLS silencing abolished SIA.
source: TetTox-mediated LHApost-dLS silencing abolished SIA (Figure 3Q and R).
evidence: This is supported by silencing experiments shown in Figure 3Q and R.

claim: LHApost-dLS neurons are functionally downstream of dLSGad1 neurons.
source: In summary, the LHApost-dLS neurons are functionally downstream of dLSGad1 neurons, and simultaneous transient activation has identical effects on nociceptive thresholds.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of effects observed with manipulation of dLS and LHA neurons.

claim: 34.2 ± 9.6% of tdTomato expressing LHApost-dLS cells were GFP positive, indicative of their excitatory status.
source: We found that 34.2 ± 9.6% (n=8 sections, 3 mice) tdTomato expressing cells (LHApost-dLS) were GFP +ve, indicative of their excitatory status (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by intersectional genetic labeling data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 28.5 ± 11.2% of tdTomato neurons in LHApost-dLS colocalized with VGlut2.
source: We found that 28.5 ± 11.2% (n=12 sections, 2 mice) tdTomato neurons colocalized with VGlut2 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: dLSGad1 neurons make synaptic connections onto VGlut2 neurons in the LHA.
source: Here, we noticed a close apposition of green synaptophysin and red gephyrin puncta in the LHA (Figure 4F), suggesting that dLSGad1 neurons make synaptic connections onto VGlut2 neurons in the LHA.
evidence: This is supported by GRASP-like synaptic labeling shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Inhibitory dLS axons target the excitatory populations of the LHA neurons.
source: Overall, these results suggest that inhibitory dLS axons target the excitatory populations of the LHA neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical data showing connections between inhibitory dLS and excitatory LHA neurons.

claim: There is little to no overlap between LHApost-dLS neurons and PV-expressing cells.
source: Since parvalbumin (PV) labels a subset of excitatory neurons in the LHA and PV-expressing neurons in the LHA have been shown to be antinociceptive (Singewald et al., 2011), we tested if LHApost-dLS neurons colocalize with PV-expressing cells and found little to no overlap between the two populations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: dLSGad1 neurons are synaptically connected with the VGlut2 +ve neurons in the LHA.
source: Together, our anatomical data indicate that the dLSGad1 neurons are synaptically connected with the VGlut2 +ve neurons in the LHA.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of anatomical tracing and synaptic marker experiments.

claim: LHApost-dLS neurons respond to acute stress caused by physical restraint.
source: Surprisingly, fiber photometry recordings showed that LHApost-dLSGCaMP6s neurons respond to acute stress caused by physical restraint and tail hanging (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry recordings shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: LHApost-dLS-GCaMP6s neurons were not engaged by noxious thermal stimuli.
source: In addition, like dLSGad1 neurons (Figure 2H–K), LHApost-dLS-GCaMP6s neurons were not engaged by noxious thermal stimuli (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry recordings shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–H.

claim: While mice struggled in the RS assay, dLSGad1-GCaMP6s neurons were active for the entire duration of the struggle bouts (up to 10 s).
source: Notably, LHApost-dLS-GCaMP6s neurons differed in their activity from the dLSGad1-GCaMP6s neurons in one aspect — while mice struggled in the RS assay, dLSGad1-GCaMP6s neurons were active for the entire duration of the struggle bouts (up to 10 s) (Figure 5D), LHApost-dLS-GCaMP6s neurons were active only during the initial phase of the struggle (1–3 s) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry recordings comparing dLS and LHA activity shown in Figure 5D.

claim: LHApost-dLS-GCaMP6s neurons were active only during the initial phase of the struggle (1–3 s).
source: Notably, LHApost-dLS-GCaMP6s neurons differed in their activity from the dLSGad1-GCaMP6s neurons in one aspect — while mice struggled in the RS assay, dLSGad1-GCaMP6s neurons were active for the entire duration of the struggle bouts (up to 10 s) (Figure 5D), LHApost-dLS-GCaMP6s neurons were active only during the initial phase of the struggle (1–3 s) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry recordings shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The activity of pre-synaptic dLS and post-synaptic LHApost-dLS neurons increases in a coordinated manner at the onset of struggle in mice undergoing RS-assay.
source: This indicates that the activity of pre-synaptic dLS and post-synaptic LHApost-dLS neurons increases in a coordinated manner at the onset of struggle in mice undergoing RS-assay.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal pattern of activity in dLS and LHA neurons during struggle.

claim: After the initial activity, LHApost-dLS neurons can potentially be suppressed by inhibitory dLS inputs causing a reduction in the firing of these post-synaptic neurons.
source: However, after the initial activity, LHApost-dLS neurons can potentially be suppressed by inhibitory dLS inputs causing a reduction in the firing of these post-synaptic neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal dynamics of activity and the known inhibitory nature of dLS-LHA connections.

claim: Acute stress inhibits a sub-population of excitatory neurons in the LHA that are postsynaptic to inhibitory dLS neurons.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that acute stress inhibits a sub-population of excitatory neurons in the LHA that are postsynaptic to inhibitory dLS neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of neural activity during stress and the anatomical connectivity.

claim: LHApost-dLS neurons have axon-terminals in the LPBN and the RVM.
source: Expression of GFP in the LHApost-dLS neurons, labeled axon-terminals in the LPBN, and the RVM (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: Activation or silencing of LPBN neurons did not alter the reflexive withdrawal thresholds or coping responses in response to noxious thermal stimuli.
source: In previous studies, activation or silencing of LPBN neurons did not alter the reflexive withdrawal thresholds or coping responses, such as licks in response to noxious thermal stimuli (Barik et al., 2018; Chiang et al., 2020; Han et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Barik et al., 2018; Chiang et al., 2020; Han et al., 2015).

claim: RVM neurons are known to modulate pain bi-directionally.
source: However, RVM neurons are known to modulate pain bi-directionally (Fields, 2004; François et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fields, 2004; François et al., 2017.

claim: SIA is opioid-dependent.
source: Importantly, SIA is opioid-dependent (Finn, 2017; Lewis et al., 1981; Vaccarino et al., 1992; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), and RVM is a major substrate for endogenous opioids (Fields, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations and naltrexone blocking experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RVM is a major substrate for endogenous opioids.
source: Importantly, SIA is opioid-dependent (Finn, 2017; Lewis et al., 1981; Vaccarino et al., 1992; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), and RVM is a major substrate for endogenous opioids (Fields, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fields, 2004.

claim: dLS-mediated SIA is opioid dependent.
source: We confirmed the opioid-dependent nature of SIA induced by septal activation, by simultaneous administration of mu-opioid receptor antagonist naltrexone and DCZ in dLSGad1-hM3Dq mice, which lead to the blocking of dLS activation-induced analgesia (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is supported by naltrexone blocking experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: The cell bodies of the RVMpost-LHA neurons were distributed in the midline area of the medulla.
source: We observed that the cell bodies of the RVMpost-LHA neurons were distributed in the midline area (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E) of the medulla.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: RVMpost-LHA neurons have abundant axon terminals in the LHA.
source: We noticed abundant axon terminals of RVMpost-LHA neurons in the LHA (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F), and projections in the deeper layers (VI/ VII) of the lumbar spinal cord (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: RVMpost-LHA neurons have projections in the deeper layers (VI/ VII) of the lumbar spinal cord.
source: We noticed abundant axon terminals of RVMpost-LHA neurons in the LHA (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F), and projections in the deeper layers (VI/ VII) of the lumbar spinal cord (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: RVMpost-LHA neurons may modulate nociceptive thresholds through their local synaptic connections within the RVM.
source: This implies that the RVMpost-LHA neurons may modulate nociceptive thresholds through their local synaptic connections within the RVM (Marchand and Hagino, 1983), recurrent connections with the PAG, or direct interactions with spinal cord neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical projections and cited literature (Marchand and Hagino, 1983).

claim: RVMpost-LHA neurons may modulate nociceptive thresholds through recurrent connections with the PAG.
source: This implies that the RVMpost-LHA neurons may modulate nociceptive thresholds through their local synaptic connections within the RVM (Marchand and Hagino, 1983), recurrent connections with the PAG, or direct interactions with spinal cord neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from known RVM-PAG connectivity patterns.

claim: RVMpost-LHA neurons may modulate nociceptive thresholds through direct interactions with spinal cord neurons.
source: This implies that the RVMpost-LHA neurons may modulate nociceptive thresholds through their local synaptic connections within the RVM (Marchand and Hagino, 1983), recurrent connections with the PAG, or direct interactions with spinal cord neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed spinal projections of RVMpost-LHA neurons.

claim: RVMpost-LHA neurons are the direct postsynaptic partners of the LHApost-dLS neurons.
source: Using the monosynaptic retrograde rabies tracing technique (Callaway and Luo, 2015; Wickersham et al., 2007), we determined if the RVMpost-LHA neurons are the direct postsynaptic partners of the LHApost-dLS neurons.
evidence: This is supported by rabies tracing experiments showing direct connections.

claim: dLS neurons are directly upstream of the RVM projecting LHA neurons.
source: Remarkably, retrogradely transported rabies-mCherry was found in the dLS neurons (Figure 6H). Indicating that the dLS neurons are directly upstream of the RVM projecting LHA neurons.
evidence: This is supported by rabies tracing data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: dLS neurons make synaptic connections with LHApre-RVM neurons.
source: Simultaneous injection of the three AAVs successfully labeled the synapses between the dLS and LHApre-RVM neurons with GFP in the LHA (Figure 6J). Thus, demonstrating that the dLS neurons make synaptic connections with LHApre-RVM neurons.
evidence: This is supported by GRASP synaptic labeling shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Calcium transients in the RVMpost-LHA neurons increased spontaneously when mice were subjected to RS.
source: Calcium transients in the RVMpost-LHA neurons increased spontaneously when the mice were subjected to RS (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry recordings shown in Figure 7C.

claim: When mice struggled under restraint, RVMpost-LHA neuronal activity was suppressed.
source: However, when the mice struggled under restraint, RVMpost-LHA neuronal activity was suppressed (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry recordings shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The activity of the RVMpost-LHA-GCaMP6s neurons increased when mice shook or licked their paws on the hot-plate test.
source: The activity of the RVMpost-LHA-GCaMP6s neurons increased when the mice shook or licked their paws on the hot-plate test (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry recordings shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The rise in activity of the RVMpost-LHA neurons preceded the licks and shakes, indicating a facilitatory role of these neurons in nocifensive behaviors.
source: Notably, the rise in activity of the RVMpost-LHA neurons preceded the licks and shakes, indicating a facilitatory role of these neurons in nocifensive behaviors.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal relationship between neural activity and behavior.

claim: RVMpost-LHA neurons started firing only once the hot plate reached noxious temperatures, with no specific activity seen at innocuous temperatures.
source: We observed that the neurons started firing only once the hot plate reached noxious temperatures, with no specific activity seen at innocuous temperatures (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry recordings during temperature gradient shown in Figure 7F.

claim: A peak in RVMpost-LHA neural firing preceded the tail-flick instance caused by thermal pain.
source: Second, we subjected the mice to the tail-flick assay and observed a peak in neural firing preceding the tail-flick instance caused by the thermal pain caused by the concentrated beam of light (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry recordings during tail-flick assay shown in Figure 7G.

claim: RVMpost-LHA neurons are pro-nociceptive and likely ON cells.
source: Thus, we hypothesized that these RVMpost-LHA neurons are pro-nociceptive and likely ON cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of activity and behavioral effects of manipulating these neurons.

claim: RVMpost-LHA neurons are activated by acute stress and suppressed when mice struggle to escape stress-causing restraint.
source: They are activated by acute stress and suppressed when the mice struggle to escape stress-causing restraint.
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry recordings during restraint stress.

claim: dLS activity increased while LHApost-dLS and RVMpost-LHA activity decreased during struggle in the RS assay.
source: When we calculated the area under the curve (AUC) of the Z-score of the recordings from the dLS, LHApost-dLS, and RVMpost-LHA neurons while the mice struggled in the RS assay, the data indicated that the dLS activity increased while at the same time LHApost-dLS, and RVMpost-LHA activity decreased (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of photometry data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The LS inhibitory neurons engaged by acute restraint suppress LH activity which in turn reduces the excitability of the pronociceptive RVM neurons and result in analgesia.
source: Together, our data indicate that the LS inhibitory neurons engaged by acute restraint, suppress LH activity which in turn reduces the excitability of the pronociceptive RVM neurons and result in analgesia.
evidence: This is the main mechanistic conclusion drawn from the combination of anatomical, recording, and manipulation experiments.

claim: Mice expressing hM3Dq in the RVMpost-LHA responded with increased licks on the hot-plate test when i.p. DCZ was administered.
source: Mice expressing hM3Dq in the RVMpost-LHA responded with increased licks on the hot-plate test and a lower latency when i.p. DCZ was administered (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This is supported by chemogenetic activation data shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: Chemogenetic silencing of RVMpost-LHA neurons reduced the number of licks on the hot-plate test.
source: Contrary to RVMpost-LHA activation, when we chemogenetically and silenced the RVMpost-LHA neurons (Figure 8E–H), the number of licks on the hot-plate test was reduced, and the latency to lick and the tail-flick latency were increased.
evidence: This is supported by chemogenetic silencing data shown in Figure 8E–H.

claim: Chemogenetic silencing of RVMpost-LHA neurons increased the latency to lick and the tail-flick latency.
source: Contrary to RVMpost-LHA activation, when we chemogenetically and silenced the RVMpost-LHA neurons (Figure 8E–H), the number of licks on the hot-plate test was reduced, and the latency to lick and the tail-flick latency were increased.
evidence: This is supported by chemogenetic silencing data shown in Figure 8E–H.

claim: Silencing bi-lateral LPBN neurons postsynaptic to LHA did not affect mouse responses on hot-plate and tail-flick tests.
source: Moreover, the observation that silencing bi-lateral LPBN neurons postsynaptic to LHA (Figure 8I and J) did not affect mouse responses on hot-plate and tail-flick tests confirmed (Figure 8K and L) that the LHA-RVM connections primarily mediate the anti-nociceptive effects of LHApost-dLS neurons.
evidence: This is supported by chemogenetic silencing data shown in Figure 8I-L.

claim: The LHA-RVM connections primarily mediate the anti-nociceptive effects of LHApost-dLS neurons.
source: Moreover, the observation that silencing bi-lateral LPBN neurons postsynaptic to LHA (Figure 8I and J) did not affect mouse responses on hot-plate and tail-flick tests confirmed (Figure 8K and L) that the LHA-RVM connections primarily mediate the anti-nociceptive effects of LHApost-dLS neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of silencing LPBN versus RVM neurons.

claim: Pro-nociceptive ON cells in the RVM can be either excitatory or inhibitory.
source: Recent observations indicate that the pro-nociceptive ON cells in the RVM can be either excitatory or inhibitory (Nguyen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nguyen et al., 2022.

claim: Activating the excitatory ON cells results in hypersensitivity to noxious stimuli.
source: Activating the excitatory ON cells results in hypersensitivity to noxious stimuli, whereas inhibiting the same neurons results in analgesia (Nguyen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nguyen et al., 2022.

claim: Inhibiting excitatory ON cells results in analgesia.
source: Activating the excitatory ON cells results in hypersensitivity to noxious stimuli, whereas inhibiting the same neurons results in analgesia (Nguyen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nguyen et al., 2022.

claim: The RVMpost-LHA neurons are excitatory.
source: Since the chemogenetic activation of the pro-nociceptive RVMpost-LHA neurons resulted in thermal hyperalgesia and inhibition leading to pain suppression, we hypothesized that the RVMpost-LHA neurons are excitatory.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral effects of manipulating these neurons and confirmed by anatomical data.

claim: There is close apposition between GFP-expressing pre-synaptic terminals from LHA and tagRFP-expressing VGlut2 expressing RVM neurons.
source: When we visualized the RVM with confocal and super-resolution microscopy (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D), we found close apposition between the GFP-expressing pre-synaptic terminals and tagRFP-expressing VGlut2 expressing RVM neurons.
evidence: This is supported by super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Excitatory LHA neurons impinge upon the excitatory RVM-ON neurons to facilitate RS-induced analgesia.
source: Thus, we concluded that the excitatory LHA neurons impinge upon the excitatory RVM-ON neurons to facilitate RS-induced analgesia.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical connectivity and functional manipulation experiments.

claim: The struggle to escape restraint engages dLS inhibitory neurons.
source: The struggle to escape restraint engages dLS inhibitory neurons.
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry recordings during struggle.

claim: Activated inhibitory dLS neurons silence excitatory LHApost-dLS neurons.
source: The activated inhibitory dLS neurons silence excitatory LHApost-dLS neurons, which consequently disengages the pro-nociceptive RVMpost-LHA neurons to drive RS-induced analgesia (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is the main mechanistic model supported by the combination of all experimental data.

claim: Silencing excitatory LHApost-dLS neurons disengages the pro-nociceptive RVMpost-LHA neurons to drive RS-induced analgesia.
source: The activated inhibitory dLS neurons silence excitatory LHApost-dLS neurons, which consequently disengages the pro-nociceptive RVMpost-LHA neurons to drive RS-induced analgesia (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is the main mechanistic model supported by the combination of all experimental data.
